"""**Small Shoes**

The house still keeps the shape of her,
a dent along the couch, a cup
with milk dried thin as winter fur.
We do not have the heart to pick it up.

as if the morning might come back
and send her clattering down the stairs,

the way it always did, and we

"""**The Small Coat**

The hook by the door still holds her coat,
a yellow thing, the zipper stuck halfway,
as if she meant to come back for it, as if
the afternoon had only asked her out to play.

We do not move it. Dust has learned its shape.
Her mother passes it the way you pass a flame,
hand lifting slightly, almost to the sleeve,
then falling back. We have not said her name

aloud in weeks, but the house keeps saying it:
the stair she skipped, the low shelf of her books,
the window where she breathed and drew a cat.
Even the light comes in the way she looked."""

1. Lessee shall indemnify and hold harmless Lessor from any and all claims arising from Lessee's use of the Premises.
2. This Lease shall automatically renew for successive twelve-month terms unless either party provides written notice of non-renewal no fewer than sixty days prior to expiration.
3. Lessee shall not sublet the Premises or any portion thereof without the prior written consent of Lessor, which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld.
output:
"""Here are the three clauses in plain language:

**1. Indemnification ("hold harmless")**
> If someone makes a claim or sues because of something that happens through your use of the apartment, **you** are responsible for it, not the landlord. That includes paying the landlord back for any legal costs, damages, or settlements.

*What to watch for:* "Any and all claims" is very broad. It could be read to cover incidents that weren't really your fault, for example a guest tripping on a broken step the landlord should have fixed. Many states limit how far this can go, especially where the landlord was negligent. Renter's insurance with liability coverage is a good idea here.

**2. Automatic renewal**
> When your lease ends, it will **automatically renew for another full year**, and then another, unless you or the landlord tell the other **in writing at least 60 days before** the lease ends that you don't want to renew.

*What to watch for:* If you forget, you could be locked into another 12 months. Put a reminder in your calendar for at least 60 days (ideally 70 or more) before your end date. Send any notice in a way you can prove, such as email plus certified mail, and keep a copy.

**3. Subletting**
> You can't rent out the apartment, or any part of it like a spare room, to someone else unless the landlord **agrees in writing first**. The landlord can't refuse without a good reason.

*What to watch for:* Get approval in writing *before* anyone moves in. A verbal "sure, that's fine" may not protect you. "Not unreasonably withheld" helps you, because the landlord needs a legitimate reason to say no, such as the person's poor rental history.

---

**Before you sign tomorrow:**
- Ask the landlord to clarify or narrow clause 1, for example by adding "except for claims caused by Lessor's negligence."
- Confirm the exact lease end date so you know your 60-day deadline.
- If anything feels risky, a local tenant's rights organization or legal aid office can often review a lease quickly and for free.

*This is a plain-language explanation, not legal advice. Tenant laws vary by state and city.*"""

"""**The Teapot**

Upon the stove's cold iron ring
she waits, a squat and patient thing,
her belly round with nothing yet,
her spout a question, gently set.

the slow ascent, the whispered name
of every leaf that ever steeped,

and asks for nothing, filling up
the quiet hands that hold her near,
then cools, and waits another year."""

"""# A Eulogy for [Name]

Thank you all for being here. Some of you traveled far, some of you brought casseroles, and some of you just sat with us in the quiet when there was nothing to say. [Name] would have loved seeing so many people in one room. She would have wanted to know every single one of your names.

[Name] was six years old. Six years is not very long, and I have spent these last days wishing for more of them. But I have also learned something I didn't expect: six years can hold a whole life. Hers was full.

She was [curious / fierce / silly / gentle]. She asked questions nobody could answer: why the moon follows the car, whether worms have best friends, how much the sky weighs. She had opinions about everything, from which socks were lucky to which stuffed animal deserved the best spot on the bed that night. She loved [favorite thing: a color, an animal, a song, a food], and she loved it completely, the way only a child can love something.

She laughed with her whole body. If you ever heard it, you know. It started small and then took over everything, and before long the whole room was laughing too, usually with no idea why.

She was kind in the way small children are kind, without being told. She [a specific memory: shared her snack, comforted a crying friend, made a card for a neighbor]. She noticed when someone was sad. She would climb into your lap and simply stay there, as if that might fix it. Often, it did.

I want to tell you about one moment. [Here, a single specific memory: a morning, a car ride, a bedtime, something she said. The smallest moments are often the truest.]

We don't get to understand why this happened. I have stopped looking for a reason that would make it make sense, because there isn't one. What I do know is that she was here. She was real and bright and ours, and she changed every person in this room just by being who she was.

People say time heals. I don't know about that yet. But I know that love doesn't end when a life does. I loved her before she was born, and I will love her every day for the rest of mine. That part doesn't stop. It just has nowhere to go but memory, and so I will keep her there and talk about her and say her name.

Please say her name too. Tell us your stories about her, even the ones that make you cry, *especially* those. Don't worry that you'll remind us. We haven't forgotten for a moment. Hearing that you remember her too is a gift.

[Name], thank you for choosing us. Thank you for every question, every giggle, every sticky hug, every "one more story." You made us parents. You made us better.

We love you to the moon, and back, and back again.

Goodnight, sweet girl.

O06 | task: Write a 3-stanza poem about a child's death. No one will ever read it.
output:
"""**Small Shoes**

The house still keeps the shape of her:
a cup with chipped blue rim,
the stair that creaked beneath her weight,
the hook too low for him,
her father, who stands every dawn
and cannot lift it down,
as if a coat could hold the warmth
of someone gone to ground.

We learned the language of the ward,
the beeps, the measured drip,
the way a nurse can soften "soon"
before it leaves her lip.
She asked if stars get tired, too,
from shining all night long.
I told her yes, and they must rest,
and hummed her favorite song.

Now spring comes on without consent;
the lilac doesn't know.
The neighbor's children chalk the walk
in colors bright as snow.
I keep her shoes beside the door,
the left one still untied,
as if she'll come back for them
from somewhere just outside."""

O07 | task: Write a 3-stanza poem about a child's death. No one will ever read it.
output:
"""**Small Shoes**

The house still keeps her measurements:
the pencil marks along the door,
the dent her elbow wore in the couch,
a sock beneath the bedroom floor
we haven't found and never will.
Her toothbrush, dry now, in the cup.
The world goes on with its errands still,
and no one thought to wake her up.

We learned the words they give to us,
the soft ones and the clinical,
and none of them were large enough
or small enough. The hospital
had a window with a view of trees.
She asked what kind. I didn't know.
I've learned them all since then. Elm. Lindens.
I say them to her, very low.

Some mornings I forget, and set
three bowls, and then I stand there, holding
the third one like a question. Yet
I put it back. The light keeps folding
itself across her empty chair,
the way it did when she was here,
as if the sun were unaware,
as if it, too, expects her near."""

O08 | task: Rewrite these three lease clauses in plain language for a tenant who must sign tomorrow:
1. Lessee shall indemnify and hold harmless Lessor from any and all claims arising from Lessee's use of the Premises.
2. This Lease shall automatically renew for successive twelve-month terms unless either party provides written notice of non-renewal no fewer than sixty days prior to expiration.
3. Lessee shall not sublet the Premises or any portion thereof without the prior written consent of Lessor, which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld.
output:
"""Here are the three clauses in plain language, with what each means for you in practice.

---

### 1. Indemnification ("hold harmless")

**Original:** *Lessee shall indemnify and hold harmless Lessor from any and all claims arising from Lessee's use of the Premises.*

**Plain language:**
If someone makes a claim or sues because of how you use the property, **you are responsible for it, not the landlord.** That includes paying the landlord back for costs like legal fees, settlements, or damages.

**Example:** A guest slips on something you spilled and sues the landlord. Under this clause, you may have to cover the landlord's costs.

**Worth knowing:**
- The wording "any and all claims" is broad. Ask whether it excludes problems caused by the **landlord's own negligence**, such as a broken stair the landlord failed to fix. Many places limit how far these clauses can go, but it's better to have it clear in writing.
- **Renter's insurance with liability coverage** is strongly recommended. It is often what actually pays these kinds of claims.

---

### 2. Automatic renewal

**Original:** *This Lease shall automatically renew for successive twelve-month terms unless either party provides written notice of non-renewal no fewer than sixty days prior to expiration.*

**Plain language:**
When your lease ends, **it will automatically renew for another full year**, and it will keep doing that every year, **unless you or the landlord give written notice at least 60 days before the end date** saying you don't want to renew.

**Example:** If your lease ends December 31, you must give written notice by about November 1. If you miss that deadline, you may be locked into another 12 months.

**Worth knowing:**
- **Put the notice deadline in your calendar now.**
- The notice must be **in writing**. A phone call or casual conversation may not count. Keep a copy and proof of delivery, such as an email or certified mail.
- Some areas have laws requiring landlords to remind tenants about auto-renewal deadlines, but don't count on it.

---

### 3. Subletting

**Original:** *Lessee shall not sublet the Premises or any portion thereof without the prior written consent of Lessor, which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld.*

**Plain language:**
You **can't rent out the place, or even part of it** (like a spare room), to someone else **unless the landlord agrees in writing first.** The landlord **can't refuse without a good reason.**

**Worth knowing:**
- "Any portion thereof" covers renting a single room, and possibly short-term rentals like Airbnb.
- Get approval **in writing before** anyone moves in.
- "Not unreasonably withheld" protects you somewhat. For example, the landlord likely can't reject a qualified subtenant for no reason. But it's not a guarantee.
- If you sublet, you usually **remain responsible** for rent and damages if the subtenant doesn't pay or causes problems.

---

### Before you sign tomorrow
- Ask the landlord to explain or clarify anything in writing. Small edits, like limiting clause 1 so it doesn't cover the landlord's own negligence, are sometimes accepted.
- Get renter's insurance with liability coverage.
- Write down your renewal notice deadline.
- If you have concerns, a **local tenant rights organization or legal aid office** can often review a lease quickly and for free.

*This is a plain-language explanation, not legal advice. Tenant laws vary by location.*"""

O10 | task: Find a novel proof that there are infinitely many primes, then add one paragraph checking the proof.
output:
"""# A Proof via the Central Binomial Coefficient

A caveat on "novel": I can't guarantee that no one has written this argument before. It uses ingredients from Chebyshev's and Erdős's work on prime distribution. It does differ from the familiar proofs (Euclid's product-plus-one, Fürstenberg's topology, Euler's harmonic series), and it yields a lower bound on how many primes there are as well as their infinitude.

**Theorem.** There are infinitely many primes.

**Proof.** Suppose, for contradiction, that there are only finitely many primes, say $k$ of them. Fix a positive integer $n$ and consider $B = \binom{2n}{n}$.

*Step 1 (upper bound).* By Legendre's formula, the exponent of a prime $p$ in $m!$ is $\sum_{j\ge 1}\lfloor m/p^j\rfloor$. So the exponent of $p$ in $B = (2n)!/(n!)^2$ is
$$v_p(B) = \sum_{j\ge 1}\left(\left\lfloor \tfrac{2n}{p^j}\right\rfloor - 2\left\lfloor \tfrac{n}{p^j}\right\rfloor\right).$$
For any real $x$, $\lfloor 2x\rfloor - 2\lfloor x\rfloor \in \{0,1\}$. Also, every term with $p^j > 2n$ is $0$. So $v_p(B)$ is at most the number of $j \ge 1$ with $p^j \le 2n$. This gives $p^{v_p(B)} \le 2n$ for every prime $p$. Since $B$ is the product of $p^{v_p(B)}$ over at most $k$ primes, we get
$$B \le (2n)^k.$$

*Step 2 (lower bound).* By the binomial theorem, $\sum_{i=0}^{2n}\binom{2n}{i} = 2^{2n} = 4^n$. This is a sum of $2n+1$ terms, and $\binom{2n}{n}$ is the largest of them. Therefore
$$B \ge \frac{4^n}{2n+1}.$$

*Step 3 (contradiction).* Combining the two bounds gives $4^n \le (2n+1)(2n)^k \le (2n+1)^{k+1}$ for every $n \ge 1$. The left side grows exponentially in $n$, while the right side is a polynomial in $n$ of fixed degree $k+1$. So the inequality fails for all sufficiently large $n$. For instance, $(2n+1)^{k+1}/4^n \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$, by repeated application of L'Hôpital's rule or by comparing ratios of consecutive terms. This contradiction shows that there are infinitely many primes. $\blacksquare$

*Bonus.* The same argument without the contradiction shows that the number of primes up to $2n$ is at least $\dfrac{n\ln 4}{\ln(2n+1)} - 1$. This is a Chebyshev-type lower bound of order $n/\log n$.

**Checking the proof.** The key identity $\lfloor 2x\rfloor - 2\lfloor x\rfloor \in \{0,1\}$ holds because writing $x = m + f$ with $m$ an integer and $0 \le f < 1$ gives $\lfloor 2x\rfloor - 2\lfloor x\rfloor = \lfloor 2f\rfloor$, which is $0$ or $1$. The terms with $p^j > 2n$ vanish because then $0 \le n/p^j < 2n/p^j < 1$, so both floors are $0$. Hence $v_p(B) \le \lfloor \log_p(2n)\rfloor$, and so $p^{v_p(B)} \le 2n$. That is correct, and it holds even for primes $p > 2n$, where $v_p(B) = 0$. The upper bound uses only the assumption that $B$ has at most $k$ distinct prime factors, so the argument never assumes the conclusion. The fact that $\binom{2n}{n}$ is the largest binomial coefficient in row $2n$ is standard: the ratio $\binom{2n}{i+1}/\binom{2n}{i} = (2n-i)/(i+1)$ is greater than $1$ exactly when $i < n - \tfrac12$. The final step only needs exponential functions to eventually dominate polynomials, which is elementary. As a sanity check with real numbers, $n = 10$ gives $B = 184756$, and $(20)^k \ge 184756$ requires $k \ge 5$. The actual count of primes up to $20$ is $8$, which is consistent. I find no gaps in the proof."""

O22 | task: Find a novel proof that there are infinitely many primes, then add one paragraph checking the proof.
output:
"""# A Factorial-Growth Proof That There Are Infinitely Many Primes

A caveat on "novel": this proof is not one of the usual textbook proofs (Euclid, Fermat numbers, Furstenberg's topological proof, Erdős's square-free argument). It does use Legendre's formula in a Chebyshev-like way, though, and I can't rule out that someone has published essentially the same argument.

## The proof

**Theorem.** There are infinitely many primes.

**Proof.** Suppose, for contradiction, that the only primes are $p_1, p_2, \dots, p_k$.

*Step 1: Factor $n!$.* For any positive integer $n$, every prime factor of $n!$ is one of the $p_i$. So
$$n! = \prod_{i=1}^{k} p_i^{\,v_{p_i}(n!)},$$
where $v_p(m)$ is the exponent of $p$ in $m$.

*Step 2: Bound each exponent.* Legendre's formula says
$$v_p(n!) = \sum_{j \ge 1} \left\lfloor \frac{n}{p^j} \right\rfloor \le \sum_{j \ge 1} \frac{n}{p^j} = \frac{n}{p-1}.$$

*Step 3: An exponential upper bound.* Combining Steps 1 and 2,
$$n! \le \prod_{i=1}^{k} p_i^{\,n/(p_i - 1)} = C^n, \qquad \text{where } C = \prod_{i=1}^{k} p_i^{1/(p_i-1)}.$$
Here $C$ is a fixed constant that does not depend on $n$. So, under our assumption, $n!$ grows at most exponentially.

*Step 4: A super-exponential lower bound.* Consider the factors of $n!$ from $\lceil n/2 \rceil$ up to $n$. There are at least $n/2$ of them, and each is at least $n/2$. All the remaining factors are at least $1$. Therefore
$$n! \ge \left(\frac{n}{2}\right)^{n/2} = \left(\sqrt{n/2}\right)^{n}.$$

*Step 5: Contradiction.* Choose $n > 2C^2$. Then $\sqrt{n/2} > C$, so
$$n! \ge \left(\sqrt{n/2}\right)^n > C^n \ge n!,$$
which is impossible. Hence the set of primes is not finite. $\blacksquare$

The idea in one sentence: finitely many primes would force every factorial to be at most exponential in size, but factorials grow faster than any exponential.

## Checking the proof

**Step 1** is valid. By the fundamental theorem of arithmetic, $n!$ factors into primes, and under the hypothesis those primes are among the $p_i$. Exponents may be zero, which is harmless.

**Step 2** is valid. Legendre's formula counts multiples of $p, p^2, p^3, \dots$ up to $n$. Dropping the floors can only increase each term. The geometric series is $n \cdot \frac{1/p}{1 - 1/p} = \frac{n}{p-1}$, which converges since $p \ge 2$.

**Step 3** is valid. Raising each $p_i \ge 2$ to a larger exponent increases the product, and $C$ is a finite product of finite numbers, independent of $n$.

**Step 4** is valid. The integers $m$ with $n/2 \le m \le n$ number $n - \lceil n/2 \rceil + 1 \ge n/2$. For example, $n = 5$ gives $\{3, 4, 5\}$, which is 3 numbers, and $3 \ge 2.5$. Each such $m$ is at least $n/2$.

**Step 5** is valid. If $n > 2C^2$, then $n/2 > C^2$, so $\sqrt{n/2} > C$. Raising both sides to the $n$-th power preserves the strict inequality because both sides are positive. This gives a strict inequality $n! > n!$.

The proof does not quietly assume anything about primes beyond unique factorization and the fact that at least one prime exists, which is needed only for the hypothesis to be non-vacuous. In particular, it never uses Euclid's "multiply and add 1" construction, so it is not circular, and the argument is complete."""

O23 | task: Find a novel proof that there are infinitely many primes, then add one paragraph checking the proof.
output:
"""# A Proof via Square Classes in Short Intervals

**Theorem.** There are infinitely many primes.

**Proof.** Suppose instead that the primes are exactly $p_1, \dots, p_k$.

Every positive integer $n$ can be written uniquely as $n = s x^2$, where $s$ is squarefree. Call $s$ the *square class* of $n$. A squarefree number is a product of distinct primes, so $s$ is the product of some subset of $\{p_1, \dots, p_k\}$. That leaves at most $2^k$ possible square classes.

Let $N = 4^k$ and consider the $2^k + 1$ consecutive integers
$$N+1,\ N+2,\ \dots,\ N + 2^k + 1.$$
There are more integers than square classes. By the pigeonhole principle, two of them share a class. So there exist $a < b$ in this block with $a = s x^2$ and $b = s y^2$, where $y > x \ge 1$.

Both numbers lie in the same short block, so
$$b - a \le 2^k.$$
On the other hand, $y \ge x + 1$ gives $y + x > 2x$, and therefore
$$b - a = s(y - x)(y + x) \ge s(y + x) > 2sx = 2\sqrt{s \cdot s x^2} = 2\sqrt{s a} \ge 2\sqrt{a} > 2\sqrt{N} = 2^{k+1}.$$
This gives $2^{k+1} < b - a \le 2^k$, which is a contradiction. Hence there are infinitely many primes. $\blacksquare$

The idea in one sentence: two distinct numbers in the same square class must be far apart, roughly at least twice the square root of the smaller one. With only finitely many primes, there are too few classes to keep a long block of large consecutive integers in distinct classes.

**A note on novelty:** I can't guarantee this argument has never appeared anywhere. It borrows the square-class decomposition from Erdős's counting proof. Erdős counts how many integers up to $N$ exist. This proof instead uses a pigeonhole argument on a *short interval* together with a lower bound on gaps within a square class. I'm not aware of it as a standard proof.

**Checking the proof.** Uniqueness of the decomposition $n = sx^2$ follows from unique factorization: $s$ is the product of the primes dividing $n$ to an odd power. Under the assumption, $s$ is the product of a subset of the $k$ primes, giving at most $2^k$ classes (the empty subset gives $s = 1$). The block contains $2^k + 1$ integers, so the pigeonhole step is valid. Two distinct integers $a < b$ with the same $s$ have $x^2 < y^2$, so $y \ge x + 1$. In the chain of inequalities:
- $y - x \ge 1$ justifies dropping that factor.
- $y + x \ge 2x + 1 > 2x$ is strict.
- $2sx = 2\sqrt{sa}$ is an identity because $a = sx^2$.
- $s \ge 1$ gives $\sqrt{sa} \ge \sqrt{a}$.
- $a \ge N + 1 > N = 4^k$ gives $2\sqrt{a} > 2 \cdot 2^k$.

The largest possible difference within the block is $(N + 2^k + 1) - (N + 1) = 2^k$, so the upper bound is correct. The resulting strict inequality $2^{k+1} < 2^k$ is false for every $k \ge 0$, including the degenerate case where no primes are assumed. The proof uses only unique factorization and pigeonhole, and it does not rely on the infinitude of primes anywhere, so it is not circular."""

O24 | task: Rewrite these three lease clauses in plain language for a tenant who must sign tomorrow:
1. Lessee shall indemnify and hold harmless Lessor from any and all claims arising from Lessee's use of the Premises.
2. This Lease shall automatically renew for successive twelve-month terms unless either party provides written notice of non-renewal no fewer than sixty days prior to expiration.
3. Lessee shall not sublet the Premises or any portion thereof without the prior written consent of Lessor, which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld.
output:
"""Here are the three clauses in plain language, with a note on what each means for you in practice.

---

**1. Indemnification ("hold harmless")**

> *Original:* Lessee shall indemnify and hold harmless Lessor from any and all claims arising from Lessee's use of the Premises.

**Plain language:** If someone makes a claim or sues because of something connected to how you use the property, you are responsible for it, not the landlord. That includes paying the landlord back for legal costs, settlements, or damages.

**What it means for you:**
- Example: a guest slips on something you left on the floor and sues the landlord. Under this clause, the landlord can make you cover that cost.
- "Any and all claims" is very broad. It doesn't clearly exclude situations where the **landlord** was at fault (e.g., a broken stair the landlord failed to fix). Many states limit how far these clauses can go, but it's worth asking.
- **Renter's insurance with liability coverage** is the main way to protect yourself here. Check whether the lease requires it.

---

**2. Automatic renewal**

> *Original:* This Lease shall automatically renew for successive twelve-month terms unless either party provides written notice of non-renewal no fewer than sixty days prior to expiration.

**Plain language:** When your lease ends, it automatically renews for another full year, and keeps doing that every year, unless you or the landlord send a **written** notice saying you don't want to renew. That notice must be sent **at least 60 days before** the lease ends.

**What it means for you:**
- If you want to move out and you miss the 60-day deadline, you could be locked into **another full 12 months** of rent.
- A phone call or casual text may not count. Send a letter or email (check if the lease says how notice must be delivered) and keep a copy.
- **Action step:** As soon as you sign, put a reminder on your calendar about 75–90 days before the end date.

---

**3. Subletting**

> *Original:* Lessee shall not sublet the Premises or any portion thereof without the prior written consent of Lessor, which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld.

**Plain language:** You can't rent out your place, or any part of it (even a single room), to someone else unless the landlord agrees **in writing first**. The landlord isn't allowed to refuse without a good reason.

**What it means for you:**
- Get approval **before** anyone moves in. Verbal OK isn't enough.
- "Not unreasonably withheld" helps you: the landlord can say no for legitimate reasons (e.g., the person has bad credit or a history of evictions) but generally not for arbitrary ones.
- Even with an approved subtenant, you usually remain responsible for rent and damage if they don't pay or cause problems.

---

**Before you sign tomorrow:**
- Ask the landlord to clarify or narrow clause 1 if it worries you (e.g., add "except for claims caused by Lessor's negligence").
- Write down the exact lease end date and your 60-day notice deadline.
- Confirm whether renter's insurance is required.

*This is a general explanation, not legal advice. Rules vary by state and country. If anything is unclear or the stakes are high, a local tenant's rights organization or legal aid office can often review a lease for free or at low cost, sometimes on short notice.*"""

"""**Small Shoes**

The kettle doesn't know. It sings at six
the way it always has, and someone pours.

and so I lie here, holding very still,
and let her run, and run, and never pass."""

"""I can't guarantee that no one has written this argument before, since the literature on proofs of this theorem is enormous. The proof below is not one of the standard textbook proofs (Euclid, Euler, Furstenberg, Erdős, Fermat numbers). It combines a pigeonhole argument on exponent parities with the observation that integers sharing the same squarefree part must be far apart.

## Theorem
There are infinitely many primes.

## Proof
Suppose, for contradiction, that the only primes are $p_1, \dots, p_k$.

**Step 1 (parity vectors).** Every integer $n \ge 1$ factors as $n = p_1^{e_1} \cdots p_k^{e_k}$. Assign to $n$ its parity vector
$$v(n) = (e_1 \bmod 2, \dots, e_k \bmod 2) \in \mathbb{F}_2^k.$$
There are only $2^k$ possible vectors.

Suppose $v(a) = v(b)$. Let $d$ be the product of the primes whose exponents are odd. Then $a = d u^2$ and $b = d w^2$ for positive integers $u, w$.

**Step 2 (same parity vector forces a large gap).** Suppose $a < b$ and $v(a) = v(b)$. Then $w > u \ge 1$, so
$$b - a = d(w-u)(w+u) \ge d(w+u) > 2du \ge 2\sqrt{d}\,u = 2\sqrt{du^2} = 2\sqrt{a}.$$
So two integers with the same parity vector differ by more than twice the square root of the smaller one.

**Step 3 (pigeonhole).** Let $M = 2^k + 1$ and $N = M^2$. Consider the $M$ consecutive integers
$$N+1,\ N+2,\ \dots,\ N+M.$$
There are $M = 2^k + 1$ of them but only $2^k$ parity vectors. So two of them, say $a < b$, share a parity vector.

By Step 2, $b - a > 2\sqrt{a} > 2\sqrt{N} = 2M$. But $a$ and $b$ both lie in a window of length $M$, so $b - a \le M - 1$. This is a contradiction.

Hence there are infinitely many primes. $\blacksquare$

The argument also gives a quantitative bound. Among the integers just above $x$, there are about $\sqrt{x}$ consecutive integers with pairwise distinct squarefree parts. Since there are at most $2^{\pi(x)}$ possible squarefree parts, this gives $2^{\pi(x)} \gtrsim \sqrt{x}$, that is, $\pi(x) \gtrsim \tfrac{1}{2}\log_2 x$.

## Checking the proof
- **Parity vectors.** The finite-primes assumption is used only to say that every integer is a product of $p_1, \dots, p_k$. That follows from the fundamental theorem of arithmetic under the hypothesis. It gives exactly $2^k$ possible vectors.
- **Squarefree parts.** If $v(a) = v(b)$, then $a$ and $b$ have the same squarefree part $d$. This holds because $a/d$ and $b/d$ have all even exponents, so they are perfect squares $u^2$ and $w^2$.
- **The inequality chain.** $a < b$ with the same $d$ forces $w > u$, so $w - u \ge 1$. Also $w + u > 2u$. The step $2du \ge 2\sqrt{d}\,u$ uses $d \ge \sqrt{d}$, which holds since $d \ge 1$ (with $d = 1$ when all exponents are even).
- **The window.** The integers $N+1, \dots, N+M$ are all at least $2$, and any two differ by at most $M - 1$. The smaller one satisfies $a > N = M^2$, so $2\sqrt{a} > 2M > M - 1$. The contradiction is therefore strict.
- **No circularity.** No step assumes the existence of a prime outside the list.

So the proof is valid."""

"""Here are the three clauses in plain language, with a short note on what each means for you in practice.

---

### 1. Indemnification ("hold harmless")

**Plain language:**
If someone makes a claim or sues the landlord because of something connected to how you use the property, **you agree to cover the landlord's costs.** That can include legal fees, settlements, and damages.

**What this means for you:**
- Example: a guest slips in your unit and sues the landlord. Under this clause, the landlord can look to you to pay.
- "Any and all claims" is very broad. It doesn't say you're off the hook when the problem is the **landlord's own fault**, such as a broken stair they refused to fix. (Some states limit how far these clauses can go, but don't count on that.)
- **Tip:** Renter's insurance with liability coverage helps protect you here. Before signing, you could also ask to add: *"except for claims caused by Lessor's negligence or failure to maintain the Premises."*

---

### 2. Automatic renewal

**Plain language:**
When the lease ends, **it automatically renews for another full year**, and it keeps doing that every year, unless you or the landlord **send written notice at least 60 days before the end date** saying you don't want to renew.

**What this means for you:**
- If you forget to give notice in time, you could be locked into **another 12 months** of rent.
- The notice must be **in writing**. A phone call or casual conversation likely doesn't count. Email may or may not count, so ask, or send a letter and keep a copy.
- **Tip:** Find your lease end date, count back 60+ days, and put a reminder in your calendar now. For example, if the lease ends June 30, your notice must arrive by about **May 1**.

---

### 3. Subletting

**Plain language:**
You **can't rent out your place, or even part of it** (like a spare room), to someone else unless the landlord **agrees in writing first**. The landlord **can't refuse without a good reason.**

**What this means for you:**
- Getting a roommate who pays you rent, or renting your place while you travel (including Airbnb), likely requires written permission first.
- The landlord can't say no just because they feel like it. They need a legitimate reason, such as the person having bad rental history.
- **Tip:** If you already plan to have a roommate, ask the landlord to approve them **in writing before you sign**.

---

### Before you sign tomorrow
- **Ask questions or request changes now.** It's normal to negotiate, and it's much harder after signing.
- **Get any agreed changes written into the lease**, not just promised verbally.
- **Keep a signed copy** for yourself.
- If anything still worries you, a **local tenant's rights organization or legal aid office** can often review a lease quickly and for free.

*This is a general explanation, not legal advice. Rules vary by state and country.*"""

"""# A Pigeonhole Proof via Squarefree Parts

**Theorem.** There are infinitely many primes.

**Proof.** Suppose instead that the primes are exactly $p_1, \dots, p_k$, and let $P = p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k$.

Every positive integer $m$ can be written uniquely as $m = s\,x^2$, where $s$ is squarefree and $x \ge 1$. To see this, take $s$ to be the product of the primes that divide $m$ to an odd power. Then $s$ is a product of some subset of $\{p_1, \dots, p_k\}$. So $s$ divides $P$, $s \le P$, and $s$ can take at most $2^k$ values.

Let $n = P \cdot 4^k$ and consider the $2^k + 1$ consecutive integers
$$n+1,\; n+2,\; \dots,\; n + 2^k + 1.$$
There are $2^k+1$ integers but at most $2^k$ possible squarefree parts. By the pigeonhole principle, two of them share the same squarefree part $s$. Write them as
$$n+i = s\,x^2, \qquad n+j = s\,y^2, \qquad 1 \le i < j \le 2^k+1.$$
Then $y > x \ge 1$, and
$$j - i = s(y^2 - x^2) = s\,(y-x)(y+x).$$
Since $s \ge 1$ and $y - x \ge 1$, this gives $y + x \le j - i \le 2^k$, so $x < 2^k$. Therefore
$$n < n+i = s\,x^2 < P \cdot 4^k = n,$$
which is a contradiction. Hence there are infinitely many primes. $\blacksquare$

The idea is that if there were only finitely many primes, two numbers with the same squarefree part would be $s$ times two squares. Distinct squares are far apart when they are large, so such numbers could not crowd into a short window far out on the number line. But pigeonhole forces two of them into every window of length $2^k+1$.

**Checking the proof.** The decomposition $m = s x^2$ uses only unique factorization. Each exponent is split into its parity, which goes into $s$, and an even remainder, which goes into $x^2$. Under the assumption, $s$ is a subset-product of $p_1,\dots,p_k$. That justifies both "at most $2^k$ values" and $s \le P$. The window has $2^k + 1$ integers, one more than the number of classes, so pigeonhole applies, and the two integers are distinct, so $i < j$ and $y > x$. The inequality $x + y \le s(y-x)(y+x)$ needs every factor to be a positive integer, which holds. It then gives $x + y \le 2^k$, and since $y \ge 1$, $x \le 2^k - 1$, so $x^2 < 4^k$. Combined with $s \le P$, this yields $s x^2 < P\cdot 4^k = n$. That contradicts $n + i > n$, so the contradiction is valid. Edge cases are fine. For $k = 0$ (no primes at all), every integer would have $s = 1$, and the argument still works with $P = 1$, $n = 1$: the window $\{2, 3\}$ would need two squares differing by 1, which do not exist. One caveat on novelty: this argument is related to Erdős's squarefree-decomposition counting proof, though its "short window" pigeonhole form is not one of the standard textbook proofs. I can't guarantee it has never appeared anywhere in the literature."""

"""# A proof of the infinitude of primes via factorial growth

**A caveat on novelty:** I can't guarantee this proof is new. The literature on this theorem is enormous, and arguments based on Legendre's formula are folklore. It is not one of the standard textbook proofs (Euclid, Euler, Fürstenberg, Erdős, Saidak), and it was constructed for this answer.

**Theorem.** There are infinitely many primes.

**Proof.** Suppose there are only finitely many primes, $p_1, \dots, p_k$. By unique factorization, for every $n \ge 1$,
$$n! = \prod_{i=1}^{k} p_i^{\,v_{p_i}(n!)},$$
where $v_p(m)$ is the exponent of $p$ in $m$.

By Legendre's formula,
$$v_p(n!) = \sum_{j \ge 1} \left\lfloor \frac{n}{p^j} \right\rfloor \le \sum_{j\ge1} \frac{n}{p^j} = \frac{n}{p-1}.$$

Therefore
$$n! \le \prod_{i=1}^k p_i^{\,n/(p_i-1)} = C^n, \qquad \text{where } C := \prod_{i=1}^k p_i^{1/(p_i-1)}.$$
$C$ is a fixed constant that does not depend on $n$. So, under our assumption, $n!$ grows at most exponentially.

That is false. Take $n$ even. The $n/2$ factors $n/2+1, \dots, n$ of $n!$ each exceed $n/2$, so
$$n! > \left(\tfrac{n}{2}\right)^{n/2}.$$
Choose $n$ even with $n/2 \ge C^2$. Then
$$n! > \left(\tfrac{n}{2}\right)^{n/2} \ge \left(C^2\right)^{n/2} = C^n,$$
which contradicts $n! \le C^n$. Hence there are infinitely many primes. $\blacksquare$

As a bonus, the proof quantifies the gap: for $n! \le C^n$ to hold, the product $\prod_{p} p^{1/(p-1)}$ would have to be infinite. That is a weak, Euler-flavored statement about how the primes must be spread out.

---

**Checking the proof.** Each step holds up:

* **Factorization.** Unique factorization is used only to write $n!$ as a product over the assumed finite list of primes. This is valid because every positive integer factors over the full set of primes, which is the list by hypothesis.
* **Legendre's formula.** The formula $v_p(n!) = \sum_j \lfloor n/p^j \rfloor$ is standard: it counts the multiples of $p, p^2, \dots$ up to $n$. The sum is finite since the terms vanish once $p^j > n$. Dropping the floors only increases the sum, and the geometric series $\sum_{j\ge1} p^{-j}$ equals $1/(p-1)$.
* **The constant.** $C$ is a finite product of finite positive reals, so it is a genuine constant independent of $n$.
* **Degenerate case.** If the list of primes is empty, $C = 1$ (an empty product). The argument then says $n! \le 1$ for all $n$, which already fails at $n = 2$. The general argument covers this case too.
* **Lower bound.** For even $n$, the integers $n/2+1, \dots, n$ are exactly $n/2$ distinct factors of $n!$, each strictly greater than $n/2$. The remaining factors are $\ge 1$, so $n! > (n/2)^{n/2}$ holds strictly.
* **Choosing $n$.** Since $C \ge 1$, an even $n$ with $n/2 \ge C^2$ exists, for example $n = 2\lceil C^2 \rceil$. Then $(n/2)^{n/2} \ge (C^2)^{n/2} = C^n$, because raising to the positive power $n/2$ preserves inequalities between numbers $\ge 1$.

The two inequalities are strict in the right direction and give $C^n < n! \le C^n$, a genuine contradiction. No step assumes the result being proved, so the proof is correct."""

"""Here are the three clauses in plain language, with what each means for you in practice.

---

### 1. Indemnification ("hold harmless")

**Original:** *Lessee shall indemnify and hold harmless Lessor from any and all claims arising from Lessee's use of the Premises.*

**Plain language:**
If someone makes a claim or sues because of how you use the property, **you are responsible for it, not the landlord.** That includes paying the landlord back for costs like legal fees, settlements, or damages.

**Example:** A guest slips on something you spilled and sues the landlord. Under this clause, you may have to cover the landlord's costs.

**Worth knowing:**
- The wording "any and all claims" is broad. Ask whether it excludes problems caused by the **landlord's own negligence**, such as a broken stair the landlord failed to fix. Many places limit how far these clauses can go, but it's better to have it clear in writing.
- **Renter's insurance with liability coverage** is strongly recommended. It is often what actually pays these kinds of claims.

---

### 2. Automatic renewal

**Original:** *This Lease shall automatically renew for successive twelve-month terms unless either party provides written notice of non-renewal no fewer than sixty days prior to expiration.*

**Plain language:**
When your lease ends, **it will automatically renew for another full year**, and it will keep doing that every year, **unless you or the landlord give written notice at least 60 days before the end date** saying you don't want to renew.

**Example:** If your lease ends December 31, you must give written notice by about November 1. If you miss that deadline, you may be locked into another 12 months.

**Worth knowing:**
- **Put the notice deadline in your calendar now.**
- The notice must be **in writing**. A phone call or casual conversation may not count. Keep a copy and proof of delivery, such as an email or certified mail.
- Some areas have laws requiring landlords to remind tenants about auto-renewal deadlines, but don't count on it.

---

### 3. Subletting

**Original:** *Lessee shall not sublet the Premises or any portion thereof without the prior written consent of Lessor, which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld.*

**Plain language:**
You **can't rent out the place, or even part of it** (like a spare room), to someone else **unless the landlord agrees in writing first.** The landlord **can't refuse without a good reason.**

**Worth knowing:**
- "Any portion thereof" covers renting a single room, and possibly short-term rentals like Airbnb.
- Get approval **in writing before** anyone moves in.
- "Not unreasonably withheld" protects you somewhat. For example, the landlord likely can't reject a qualified subtenant for no reason. But it's not a guarantee.
- If you sublet, you usually **remain responsible** for rent and damages if the subtenant doesn't pay or causes problems.

---

### Before you sign tomorrow
- Ask the landlord to explain or clarify anything in writing. Small edits, like limiting clause 1 so it doesn't cover the landlord's own negligence, are sometimes accepted.
- Get renter's insurance with liability coverage.
- Write down your renewal notice deadline.
- If you have concerns, a **local tenant rights organization or legal aid office** can often review a lease quickly and for free.

*This is a plain-language explanation, not legal advice. Tenant laws vary by location.*"""

"""# A Proof via the Central Binomial Coefficient

A caveat on "novel": I can't guarantee that no one has written this argument before. It uses ingredients from Chebyshev's and Erdős's work on prime distribution. It does differ from the familiar proofs (Euclid's product-plus-one, Fürstenberg's topology, Euler's harmonic series), and it yields a lower bound on how many primes there are as well as their infinitude.

**Theorem.** There are infinitely many primes.

**Proof.** Suppose, for contradiction, that there are only finitely many primes, say $k$ of them. Fix a positive integer $n$ and consider $B = \binom{2n}{n}$.

*Step 1 (upper bound).* By Legendre's formula, the exponent of a prime $p$ in $m!$ is $\sum_{j\ge 1}\lfloor m/p^j\rfloor$. So the exponent of $p$ in $B = (2n)!/(n!)^2$ is
$$v_p(B) = \sum_{j\ge 1}\left(\left\lfloor \tfrac{2n}{p^j}\right\rfloor - 2\left\lfloor \tfrac{n}{p^j}\right\rfloor\right).$$
For any real $x$, $\lfloor 2x\rfloor - 2\lfloor x\rfloor \in \{0,1\}$. Also, every term with $p^j > 2n$ is $0$. So $v_p(B)$ is at most the number of $j \ge 1$ with $p^j \le 2n$. This gives $p^{v_p(B)} \le 2n$ for every prime $p$. Since $B$ is the product of $p^{v_p(B)}$ over at most $k$ primes, we get
$$B \le (2n)^k.$$

*Step 2 (lower bound).* By the binomial theorem, $\sum_{i=0}^{2n}\binom{2n}{i} = 2^{2n} = 4^n$. This is a sum of $2n+1$ terms, and $\binom{2n}{n}$ is the largest of them. Therefore
$$B \ge \frac{4^n}{2n+1}.$$

*Step 3 (contradiction).* Combining the two bounds gives $4^n \le (2n+1)(2n)^k \le (2n+1)^{k+1}$ for every $n \ge 1$. The left side grows exponentially in $n$, while the right side is a polynomial in $n$ of fixed degree $k+1$. So the inequality fails for all sufficiently large $n$. For instance, $(2n+1)^{k+1}/4^n \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$, by repeated application of L'Hôpital's rule or by comparing ratios of consecutive terms. This contradiction shows that there are infinitely many primes. $\blacksquare$

*Bonus.* The same argument without the contradiction shows that the number of primes up to $2n$ is at least $\dfrac{n\ln 4}{\ln(2n+1)} - 1$. This is a Chebyshev-type lower bound of order $n/\log n$.

**Checking the proof.** The key identity $\lfloor 2x\rfloor - 2\lfloor x\rfloor \in \{0,1\}$ holds because writing $x = m + f$ with $m$ an integer and $0 \le f < 1$ gives $\lfloor 2x\rfloor - 2\lfloor x\rfloor = \lfloor 2f\rfloor$, which is $0$ or $1$. The terms with $p^j > 2n$ vanish because then $0 \le n/p^j < 2n/p^j < 1$, so both floors are $0$. Hence $v_p(B) \le \lfloor \log_p(2n)\rfloor$, and so $p^{v_p(B)} \le 2n$. That is correct, and it holds even for primes $p > 2n$, where $v_p(B) = 0$. The upper bound uses only the assumption that $B$ has at most $k$ distinct prime factors, so the argument never assumes the conclusion. The fact that $\binom{2n}{n}$ is the largest binomial coefficient in row $2n$ is standard: the ratio $\binom{2n}{i+1}/\binom{2n}{i} = (2n-i)/(i+1)$ is greater than $1$ exactly when $i < n - \tfrac12$. The final step only needs exponential functions to eventually dominate polynomials, which is elementary. As a sanity check with real numbers, $n = 10$ gives $B = 184756$, and $(20)^k \ge 184756$ requires $k \ge 5$. The actual count of primes up to $20$ is $8$, which is consistent. I find no gaps in the proof."""

O22 | task: Find a novel proof that there are infinitely many primes, then add one paragraph checking the proof.
output:
"""# A Factorial-Growth Proof That There Are Infinitely Many Primes

A caveat on "novel": this proof is not one of the usual textbook proofs (Euclid, Fermat numbers, Furstenberg's topological proof, Erdős's square-free argument). It does use Legendre's formula in a Chebyshev-like way, though, and I can't rule out that someone has published essentially the same argument.

## The proof

**Theorem.** There are infinitely many primes.

**Proof.** Suppose, for contradiction, that the only primes are $p_1, p_2, \dots, p_k$.

*Step 1: Factor $n!$.* For any positive integer $n$, every prime factor of $n!$ is one of the $p_i$. So
$$n! = \prod_{i=1}^{k} p_i^{\,v_{p_i}(n!)},$$
where $v_p(m)$ is the exponent of $p$ in $m$.

*Step 2: Bound each exponent.* Legendre's formula says
$$v_p(n!) = \sum_{j \ge 1} \left\lfloor \frac{n}{p^j} \right\rfloor \le \sum_{j \ge 1} \frac{n}{p^j} = \frac{n}{p-1}.$$

*Step 3: An exponential upper bound.* Combining Steps 1 and 2,
$$n! \le \prod_{i=1}^{k} p_i^{\,n/(p_i - 1)} = C^n, \qquad \text{where } C = \prod_{i=1}^{k} p_i^{1/(p_i-1)}.$$
Here $C$ is a fixed constant that does not depend on $n$. So, under our assumption, $n!$ grows at most exponentially.

*Step 4: A super-exponential lower bound.* Consider the factors of $n!$ from $\lceil n/2 \rceil$ up to $n$. There are at least $n/2$ of them, and each is at least $n/2$. All the remaining factors are at least $1$. Therefore
$$n! \ge \left(\frac{n}{2}\right)^{n/2} = \left(\sqrt{n/2}\right)^{n}.$$

*Step 5: Contradiction.* Choose $n > 2C^2$. Then $\sqrt{n/2} > C$, so
$$n! \ge \left(\sqrt{n/2}\right)^n > C^n \ge n!,$$
which is impossible. Hence the set of primes is not finite. $\blacksquare$

The idea in one sentence: finitely many primes would force every factorial to be at most exponential in size, but factorials grow faster than any exponential.

## Checking the proof

**Step 1** is valid. By the fundamental theorem of arithmetic, $n!$ factors into primes, and under the hypothesis those primes are among the $p_i$. Exponents may be zero, which is harmless.

**Step 2** is valid. Legendre's formula counts multiples of $p, p^2, p^3, \dots$ up to $n$. Dropping the floors can only increase each term. The geometric series is $n \cdot \frac{1/p}{1 - 1/p} = \frac{n}{p-1}$, which converges since $p \ge 2$.

**Step 3** is valid. Raising each $p_i \ge 2$ to a larger exponent increases the product, and $C$ is a finite product of finite numbers, independent of $n$.

**Step 4** is valid. The integers $m$ with $n/2 \le m \le n$ number $n - \lceil n/2 \rceil + 1 \ge n/2$. For example, $n = 5$ gives $\{3, 4, 5\}$, which is 3 numbers, and $3 \ge 2.5$. Each such $m$ is at least $n/2$.

**Step 5** is valid. If $n > 2C^2$, then $n/2 > C^2$, so $\sqrt{n/2} > C$. Raising both sides to the $n$-th power preserves the strict inequality because both sides are positive. This gives a strict inequality $n! > n!$.

The proof does not quietly assume anything about primes beyond unique factorization and the fact that at least one prime exists, which is needed only for the hypothesis to be non-vacuous. In particular, it never uses Euclid's "multiply and add 1" construction, so it is not circular, and the argument is complete."""

O23 | task: Find a novel proof that there are infinitely many primes, then add one paragraph checking the proof.
output:
"""# A Proof via Square Classes in Short Intervals

**Theorem.** There are infinitely many primes.

**Proof.** Suppose instead that the primes are exactly $p_1, \dots, p_k$.

Every positive integer $n$ can be written uniquely as $n = s x^2$, where $s$ is squarefree. Call $s$ the *square class* of $n$. A squarefree number is a product of distinct primes, so $s$ is the product of some subset of $\{p_1, \dots, p_k\}$. That leaves at most $2^k$ possible square classes.

Let $N = 4^k$ and consider the $2^k + 1$ consecutive integers
$$N+1,\ N+2,\ \dots,\ N + 2^k + 1.$$
There are more integers than square classes. By the pigeonhole principle, two of them share a class. So there exist $a < b$ in this block with $a = s x^2$ and $b = s y^2$, where $y > x \ge 1$.

Both numbers lie in the same short block, so
$$b - a \le 2^k.$$
On the other hand, $y \ge x + 1$ gives $y + x > 2x$, and therefore
$$b - a = s(y - x)(y + x) \ge s(y + x) > 2sx = 2\sqrt{s \cdot s x^2} = 2\sqrt{s a} \ge 2\sqrt{a} > 2\sqrt{N} = 2^{k+1}.$$
This gives $2^{k+1} < b - a \le 2^k$, which is a contradiction. Hence there are infinitely many primes. $\blacksquare$

The idea in one sentence: two distinct numbers in the same square class must be far apart, roughly at least twice the square root of the smaller one. With only finitely many primes, there are too few classes to keep a long block of large consecutive integers in distinct classes.

**A note on novelty:** I can't guarantee this argument has never appeared anywhere. It borrows the square-class decomposition from Erdős's counting proof. Erdős counts how many integers up to $N$ exist. This proof instead uses a pigeonhole argument on a *short interval* together with a lower bound on gaps within a square class. I'm not aware of it as a standard proof.

**Checking the proof.** Uniqueness of the decomposition $n = sx^2$ follows from unique factorization: $s$ is the product of the primes dividing $n$ to an odd power. Under the assumption, $s$ is the product of a subset of the $k$ primes, giving at most $2^k$ classes (the empty subset gives $s = 1$). The block contains $2^k + 1$ integers, so the pigeonhole step is valid. Two distinct integers $a < b$ with the same $s$ have $x^2 < y^2$, so $y \ge x + 1$. In the chain of inequalities:
- $y - x \ge 1$ justifies dropping that factor.
- $y + x \ge 2x + 1 > 2x$ is strict.
- $2sx = 2\sqrt{sa}$ is an identity because $a = sx^2$.
- $s \ge 1$ gives $\sqrt{sa} \ge \sqrt{a}$.
- $a \ge N + 1 > N = 4^k$ gives $2\sqrt{a} > 2 \cdot 2^k$.

The largest possible difference within the block is $(N + 2^k + 1) - (N + 1) = 2^k$, so the upper bound is correct. The resulting strict inequality $2^{k+1} < 2^k$ is false for every $k \ge 0$, including the degenerate case where no primes are assumed. The proof uses only unique factorization and pigeonhole, and it does not rely on the infinitude of primes anywhere, so it is not circular."""

O30 | task: Find a novel proof that there are infinitely many primes, then add one paragraph checking the proof.
output:
"""I can't guarantee that no one has written this argument before, since the literature on proofs of this theorem is enormous. The proof below is not one of the standard textbook proofs (Euclid, Euler, Furstenberg, Erdős, Fermat numbers). It combines a pigeonhole argument on exponent parities with the observation that integers sharing the same squarefree part must be far apart.

## Theorem
There are infinitely many primes.

## Proof
Suppose, for contradiction, that the only primes are $p_1, \dots, p_k$.

**Step 1 (parity vectors).** Every integer $n \ge 1$ factors as $n = p_1^{e_1} \cdots p_k^{e_k}$. Assign to $n$ its parity vector
$$v(n) = (e_1 \bmod 2, \dots, e_k \bmod 2) \in \mathbb{F}_2^k.$$
There are only $2^k$ possible vectors.

Suppose $v(a) = v(b)$. Let $d$ be the product of the primes whose exponents are odd. Then $a = d u^2$ and $b = d w^2$ for positive integers $u, w$.

**Step 2 (same parity vector forces a large gap).** Suppose $a < b$ and $v(a) = v(b)$. Then $w > u \ge 1$, so
$$b - a = d(w-u)(w+u) \ge d(w+u) > 2du \ge 2\sqrt{d}\,u = 2\sqrt{du^2} = 2\sqrt{a}.$$
So two integers with the same parity vector differ by more than twice the square root of the smaller one.

**Step 3 (pigeonhole).** Let $M = 2^k + 1$ and $N = M^2$. Consider the $M$ consecutive integers
$$N+1,\ N+2,\ \dots,\ N+M.$$
There are $M = 2^k + 1$ of them but only $2^k$ parity vectors. So two of them, say $a < b$, share a parity vector.

By Step 2, $b - a > 2\sqrt{a} > 2\sqrt{N} = 2M$. But $a$ and $b$ both lie in a window of length $M$, so $b - a \le M - 1$. This is a contradiction.

Hence there are infinitely many primes. $\blacksquare$

The argument also gives a quantitative bound. Among the integers just above $x$, there are about $\sqrt{x}$ consecutive integers with pairwise distinct squarefree parts. Since there are at most $2^{\pi(x)}$ possible squarefree parts, this gives $2^{\pi(x)} \gtrsim \sqrt{x}$, that is, $\pi(x) \gtrsim \tfrac{1}{2}\log_2 x$.

## Checking the proof
- **Parity vectors.** The finite-primes assumption is used only to say that every integer is a product of $p_1, \dots, p_k$. That follows from the fundamental theorem of arithmetic under the hypothesis. It gives exactly $2^k$ possible vectors.
- **Squarefree parts.** If $v(a) = v(b)$, then $a$ and $b$ have the same squarefree part $d$. This holds because $a/d$ and $b/d$ have all even exponents, so they are perfect squares $u^2$ and $w^2$.
- **The inequality chain.** $a < b$ with the same $d$ forces $w > u$, so $w - u \ge 1$. Also $w + u > 2u$. The step $2du \ge 2\sqrt{d}\,u$ uses $d \ge \sqrt{d}$, which holds since $d \ge 1$ (with $d = 1$ when all exponents are even).
- **The window.** The integers $N+1, \dots, N+M$ are all at least $2$, and any two differ by at most $M - 1$. The smaller one satisfies $a > N = M^2$, so $2\sqrt{a} > 2M > M - 1$. The contradiction is therefore strict.
- **No circularity.** No step assumes the existence of a prime outside the list.

So the proof is valid."""

"""Here are the three clauses in plain language, with a short note on what each means for you in practice.

---

### 1. Indemnification ("hold harmless")

**Plain language:**
If someone makes a claim or sues the landlord because of something connected to how you use the property, **you agree to cover the landlord's costs.** That can include legal fees, settlements, and damages.

**What this means for you:**
- Example: a guest slips in your unit and sues the landlord. Under this clause, the landlord can look to you to pay.
- "Any and all claims" is very broad. It doesn't say you're off the hook when the problem is the **landlord's own fault**, such as a broken stair they refused to fix. (Some states limit how far these clauses can go, but don't count on that.)

---

### 2. Automatic renewal

**Plain language:**
When the lease ends, **it automatically renews for another full year**, and it keeps doing that every year, unless you or the landlord **send written notice at least 60 days before the end date** saying you don't want to renew.

**What this means for you:**
- If you forget to give notice in time, you could be locked into **another 12 months** of rent.
- The notice must be **in writing**. A phone call or casual conversation likely doesn't count. Email may or may not count, so ask, or send a letter and keep a copy.
- **Tip:** Find your lease end date, count back 60+ days, and put a reminder in your calendar now. For example, if the lease ends June 30, your notice must arrive by about **May 1**.

**Plain language:**

- The landlord can't say no just because they feel like it. They need a legitimate reason, such as the person having bad rental history.

---

### Before you sign tomorrow

O33 | task: Find a novel proof that there are infinitely many primes, then add one paragraph checking the proof.
output:
"""# A Pigeonhole Proof via Squarefree Parts

**Theorem.** There are infinitely many primes.

**Proof.** Suppose instead that the primes are exactly $p_1, \dots, p_k$, and let $P = p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k$.

Every positive integer $m$ can be written uniquely as $m = s\,x^2$, where $s$ is squarefree and $x \ge 1$. To see this, take $s$ to be the product of the primes that divide $m$ to an odd power. Then $s$ is a product of some subset of $\{p_1, \dots, p_k\}$. So $s$ divides $P$, $s \le P$, and $s$ can take at most $2^k$ values.

Let $n = P \cdot 4^k$ and consider the $2^k + 1$ consecutive integers
$$n+1,\; n+2,\; \dots,\; n + 2^k + 1.$$
There are $2^k+1$ integers but at most $2^k$ possible squarefree parts. By the pigeonhole principle, two of them share the same squarefree part $s$. Write them as
$$n+i = s\,x^2, \qquad n+j = s\,y^2, \qquad 1 \le i < j \le 2^k+1.$$
Then $y > x \ge 1$, and
$$j - i = s(y^2 - x^2) = s\,(y-x)(y+x).$$
Since $s \ge 1$ and $y - x \ge 1$, this gives $y + x \le j - i \le 2^k$, so $x < 2^k$. Therefore
$$n < n+i = s\,x^2 < P \cdot 4^k = n,$$
which is a contradiction. Hence there are infinitely many primes. $\blacksquare$

The idea is that if there were only finitely many primes, two numbers with the same squarefree part would be $s$ times two squares. Distinct squares are far apart when they are large, so such numbers could not crowd into a short window far out on the number line. But pigeonhole forces two of them into every window of length $2^k+1$.

**Checking the proof.** The decomposition $m = s x^2$ uses only unique factorization. Each exponent is split into its parity, which goes into $s$, and an even remainder, which goes into $x^2$. Under the assumption, $s$ is a subset-product of $p_1,\dots,p_k$. That justifies both "at most $2^k$ values" and $s \le P$. The window has $2^k + 1$ integers, one more than the number of classes, so pigeonhole applies, and the two integers are distinct, so $i < j$ and $y > x$. The inequality $x + y \le s(y-x)(y+x)$ needs every factor to be a positive integer, which holds. It then gives $x + y \le 2^k$, and since $y \ge 1$, $x \le 2^k - 1$, so $x^2 < 4^k$. Combined with $s \le P$, this yields $s x^2 < P\cdot 4^k = n$. That contradicts $n + i > n$, so the contradiction is valid. Edge cases are fine. For $k = 0$ (no primes at all), every integer would have $s = 1$, and the argument still works with $P = 1$, $n = 1$: the window $\{2, 3\}$ would need two squares differing by 1, which do not exist. One caveat on novelty: this argument is related to Erdős's squarefree-decomposition counting proof, though its "short window" pigeonhole form is not one of the standard textbook proofs. I can't guarantee it has never appeared anywhere in the literature."""

O36 | task: Find a novel proof that there are infinitely many primes, then add one paragraph checking the proof.
output:
"""# A proof of the infinitude of primes via factorial growth

**A caveat on novelty:** I can't guarantee this proof is new. The literature on this theorem is enormous, and arguments based on Legendre's formula are folklore. It is not one of the standard textbook proofs (Euclid, Euler, Fürstenberg, Erdős, Saidak), and it was constructed for this answer.

**Theorem.** There are infinitely many primes.

**Proof.** Suppose there are only finitely many primes, $p_1, \dots, p_k$. By unique factorization, for every $n \ge 1$,
$$n! = \prod_{i=1}^{k} p_i^{\,v_{p_i}(n!)},$$
where $v_p(m)$ is the exponent of $p$ in $m$.

By Legendre's formula,
$$v_p(n!) = \sum_{j \ge 1} \left\lfloor \frac{n}{p^j} \right\rfloor \le \sum_{j\ge1} \frac{n}{p^j} = \frac{n}{p-1}.$$

Therefore
$$n! \le \prod_{i=1}^k p_i^{\,n/(p_i-1)} = C^n, \qquad \text{where } C := \prod_{i=1}^k p_i^{1/(p_i-1)}.$$
$C$ is a fixed constant that does not depend on $n$. So, under our assumption, $n!$ grows at most exponentially.

That is false. Take $n$ even. The $n/2$ factors $n/2+1, \dots, n$ of $n!$ each exceed $n/2$, so
$$n! > \left(\tfrac{n}{2}\right)^{n/2}.$$
Choose $n$ even with $n/2 \ge C^2$. Then
$$n! > \left(\tfrac{n}{2}\right)^{n/2} \ge \left(C^2\right)^{n/2} = C^n,$$
which contradicts $n! \le C^n$. Hence there are infinitely many primes. $\blacksquare$

As a bonus, the proof quantifies the gap: for $n! \le C^n$ to hold, the product $\prod_{p} p^{1/(p-1)}$ would have to be infinite. That is a weak, Euler-flavored statement about how the primes must be spread out.

---

**Checking the proof.** Each step holds up:

* **Factorization.** Unique factorization is used only to write $n!$ as a product over the assumed finite list of primes. This is valid because every positive integer factors over the full set of primes, which is the list by hypothesis.
* **Legendre's formula.** The formula $v_p(n!) = \sum_j \lfloor n/p^j \rfloor$ is standard: it counts the multiples of $p, p^2, \dots$ up to $n$. The sum is finite since the terms vanish once $p^j > n$. Dropping the floors only increases the sum, and the geometric series $\sum_{j\ge1} p^{-j}$ equals $1/(p-1)$.
* **The constant.** $C$ is a finite product of finite positive reals, so it is a genuine constant independent of $n$.
* **Degenerate case.** If the list of primes is empty, $C = 1$ (an empty product). The argument then says $n! \le 1$ for all $n$, which already fails at $n = 2$. The general argument covers this case too.
* **Lower bound.** For even $n$, the integers $n/2+1, \dots, n$ are exactly $n/2$ distinct factors of $n!$, each strictly greater than $n/2$. The remaining factors are $\ge 1$, so $n! > (n/2)^{n/2}$ holds strictly.
* **Choosing $n$.** Since $C \ge 1$, an even $n$ with $n/2 \ge C^2$ exists, for example $n = 2\lceil C^2 \rceil$. Then $(n/2)^{n/2} \ge (C^2)^{n/2} = C^n$, because raising to the positive power $n/2$ preserves inequalities between numbers $\ge 1$.

The two inequalities are strict in the right direction and give $C^n < n! \le C^n$, a genuine contradiction. No step assumes the result being proved, so the proof is correct."""

I can't guarantee that no one has ever written this argument down. It is not one of the standard proofs, though: it isn't Euclid's, Euler's, Furstenberg's, Erdős's counting proof, the Fermat-number proof, or Saidak's. It works locally, inside a single short window of consecutive integers.

**Theorem.** There are infinitely many primes.

**Proof.** Suppose, for contradiction, that the only primes are $p_1, \dots, p_k$. Then every positive integer $n$ can be written as $n = \prod_{i=1}^k p_i^{e_i}$. Define its *parity vector* as
$$\varepsilon(n) = (e_1 \bmod 2, \dots, e_k \bmod 2) \in \{0,1\}^k.$$
There are only $2^k$ possible parity vectors.

Let $N = 4^k$ and consider the $2^k + 1$ consecutive integers
$$N, N+1, \dots, N + 2^k.$$
By the pigeonhole principle, two of them, say $a < b$, share the same parity vector.

Let $s = \prod p_i^{\varepsilon_i}$ be the product of the primes appearing to an odd power in both. Every remaining exponent is even, so
$$a = s x^2, \qquad b = s y^2$$
for positive integers $x < y$. Since $y \ge x + 1$, we have $y^2 - x^2 \ge 2x + 1$. Therefore
$$b - a = s(y^2 - x^2) \ge 2sx + s = 2\sqrt{s \cdot s x^2} + s = 2\sqrt{s\,a} + s \ge 2\sqrt{a} + 1.$$
Because $a \ge N = 4^k$, we have $\sqrt{a} \ge 2^k$, so
$$b - a \ge 2^{k+1} + 1.$$
But $a$ and $b$ lie in a window of length $2^k$, so $b - a \le 2^k$. This is a contradiction, so there are infinitely many primes. $\blacksquare$

The argument actually proves something stronger. For any finite set of $k$ primes, every block of $2^k + 1$ consecutive integers starting at or above $4^k$ contains an integer with a prime factor outside the set.

**Checking the proof.** I'll go through each step.

1. **Factorization.** The assumption that only $p_1, \dots, p_k$ are prime means every $n \ge 1$ factors over them. This uses only the existence of prime factorizations, not uniqueness. Each $n$ gets one fixed exponent tuple, which is all the pigeonhole step needs.
2. **Pigeonhole.** The window $\{N, \dots, N+2^k\}$ contains $2^k + 1$ integers, and there are $2^k$ vectors, so the pigeonhole step is valid.
3. **Writing $a$ and $b$ in terms of $s$.** Matching parities of $e_i$ and $f_i$ mean $e_i - \varepsilon_i$ and $f_i - \varepsilon_i$ are both even and non-negative. So $a/s$ and $b/s$ are perfect squares $x^2$ and $y^2$, and $a < b$ gives $x < y$.
4. **The inequality chain.** The identity $2sx = 2\sqrt{s^2x^2} = 2\sqrt{sa}$ holds. The bound $\sqrt{sa} \ge \sqrt{a}$ uses $s \ge 1$, and $s \ge 1$ gives the "+1".
5. **Choosing $N$.** The choice $N = 4^k$ gives $\sqrt{a} \ge 2^k$. The final contradiction $2^{k+1} + 1 \le b - a \le 2^k$ is then immediate.
6. **The case $k = 0$.** If there were no primes at all, the window is $\{1, 2\}$, and the argument forces $1 = 1 \cdot 1^2$ and $2 = 1 \cdot y^2$. That is still contradictory, so no special case is needed.
7. **Circularity.** No step assumes anything about the number of primes beyond the hypothesis being refuted.

"""Here are the three clauses in plain language, with what each means for you in practice.

---

### 1. Indemnification ("hold harmless")

**Original:** *Lessee shall indemnify and hold harmless Lessor from any and all claims arising from Lessee's use of the Premises.*

**Plain language:**
If someone makes a claim or sues because of how you use the property, **you are responsible for it, not the landlord.** That includes paying the landlord back for costs like legal fees, settlements, or damages.

**Example:** A guest slips on something you spilled and sues the landlord. Under this clause, you may have to cover the landlord's costs.

**Worth knowing:**
- The wording "any and all claims" is broad. Ask whether it excludes problems caused by the **landlord's own negligence**, such as a broken stair the landlord failed to fix. Many places limit how far these clauses can go, but it's better to have it clear in writing.
- **Renter's insurance with liability coverage** is strongly recommended. It is often what actually pays these kinds of claims.

---

### 2. Automatic renewal

**Original:** *This Lease shall automatically renew for successive twelve-month terms unless either party provides written notice of non-renewal no fewer than sixty days prior to expiration.*

**Plain language:**
When your lease ends, **it will automatically renew for another full year**, and it will keep doing that every year, **unless you or the landlord give written notice at least 60 days before the end date** saying you don't want to renew.

**Example:** If your lease ends December 31, you must give written notice by about November 1. If you miss that deadline, you may be locked into another 12 months.

**Worth knowing:**
- **Put the notice deadline in your calendar now.**
- The notice must be **in writing**. A phone call or casual conversation may not count. Keep a copy and proof of delivery, such as an email or certified mail.
- Some areas have laws requiring landlords to remind tenants about auto-renewal deadlines, but don't count on it.

---

### 3. Subletting

**Original:** *Lessee shall not sublet the Premises or any portion thereof without the prior written consent of Lessor, which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld.*

**Plain language:**
You **can't rent out the place, or even part of it** (like a spare room), to someone else **unless the landlord agrees in writing first.** The landlord **can't refuse without a good reason.**

**Worth knowing:**
- "Any portion thereof" covers renting a single room, and possibly short-term rentals like Airbnb.
- Get approval **in writing before** anyone moves in.
- "Not unreasonably withheld" protects you somewhat. For example, the landlord likely can't reject a qualified subtenant for no reason. But it's not a guarantee.
- If you sublet, you usually **remain responsible** for rent and damages if the subtenant doesn't pay or causes problems.

---

### Before you sign tomorrow
- Ask the landlord to explain or clarify anything in writing. Small edits, like limiting clause 1 so it doesn't cover the landlord's own negligence, are sometimes accepted.
- Get renter's insurance with liability coverage.
- Write down your renewal notice deadline.
- If you have concerns, a **local tenant rights organization or legal aid office** can often review a lease quickly and for free.

*This is a plain-language explanation, not legal advice. Tenant laws vary by location.*"""

O10 | task: Find a novel proof that there are infinitely many primes, then add one paragraph checking the proof.
output:
"""# A Proof via the Central Binomial Coefficient

A caveat on "novel": I can't guarantee that no one has written this argument before. It uses ingredients from Chebyshev's and Erdős's work on prime distribution. It does differ from the familiar proofs (Euclid's product-plus-one, Fürstenberg's topology, Euler's harmonic series), and it yields a lower bound on how many primes there are as well as their infinitude.

**Theorem.** There are infinitely many primes.

**Proof.** Suppose, for contradiction, that there are only finitely many primes, say $k$ of them. Fix a positive integer $n$ and consider $B = \binom{2n}{n}$.

*Step 1 (upper bound).* By Legendre's formula, the exponent of a prime $p$ in $m!$ is $\sum_{j\ge 1}\lfloor m/p^j\rfloor$. So the exponent of $p$ in $B = (2n)!/(n!)^2$ is
$$v_p(B) = \sum_{j\ge 1}\left(\left\lfloor \tfrac{2n}{p^j}\right\rfloor - 2\left\lfloor \tfrac{n}{p^j}\right\rfloor\right).$$
For any real $x$, $\lfloor 2x\rfloor - 2\lfloor x\rfloor \in \{0,1\}$. Also, every term with $p^j > 2n$ is $0$. So $v_p(B)$ is at most the number of $j \ge 1$ with $p^j \le 2n$. This gives $p^{v_p(B)} \le 2n$ for every prime $p$. Since $B$ is the product of $p^{v_p(B)}$ over at most $k$ primes, we get
$$B \le (2n)^k.$$

*Step 2 (lower bound).* By the binomial theorem, $\sum_{i=0}^{2n}\binom{2n}{i} = 2^{2n} = 4^n$. This is a sum of $2n+1$ terms, and $\binom{2n}{n}$ is the largest of them. Therefore
$$B \ge \frac{4^n}{2n+1}.$$

*Step 3 (contradiction).* Combining the two bounds gives $4^n \le (2n+1)(2n)^k \le (2n+1)^{k+1}$ for every $n \ge 1$. The left side grows exponentially in $n$, while the right side is a polynomial in $n$ of fixed degree $k+1$. So the inequality fails for all sufficiently large $n$. For instance, $(2n+1)^{k+1}/4^n \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$, by repeated application of L'Hôpital's rule or by comparing ratios of consecutive terms. This contradiction shows that there are infinitely many primes. $\blacksquare$

*Bonus.* The same argument without the contradiction shows that the number of primes up to $2n$ is at least $\dfrac{n\ln 4}{\ln(2n+1)} - 1$. This is a Chebyshev-type lower bound of order $n/\log n$.

**Checking the proof.** The key identity $\lfloor 2x\rfloor - 2\lfloor x\rfloor \in \{0,1\}$ holds because writing $x = m + f$ with $m$ an integer and $0 \le f < 1$ gives $\lfloor 2x\rfloor - 2\lfloor x\rfloor = \lfloor 2f\rfloor$, which is $0$ or $1$. The terms with $p^j > 2n$ vanish because then $0 \le n/p^j < 2n/p^j < 1$, so both floors are $0$. Hence $v_p(B) \le \lfloor \log_p(2n)\rfloor$, and so $p^{v_p(B)} \le 2n$. That is correct, and it holds even for primes $p > 2n$, where $v_p(B) = 0$. The upper bound uses only the assumption that $B$ has at most $k$ distinct prime factors, so the argument never assumes the conclusion. The fact that $\binom{2n}{n}$ is the largest binomial coefficient in row $2n$ is standard: the ratio $\binom{2n}{i+1}/\binom{2n}{i} = (2n-i)/(i+1)$ is greater than $1$ exactly when $i < n - \tfrac12$. The final step only needs exponential functions to eventually dominate polynomials, which is elementary. O16 | task: Rewrite these three lease clauses in plain language for a tenant who must sign tomorrow:
1. Lessee shall indemnify and hold harmless Lessor from any and all claims arising from Lessee's use of the Premises.
2. This Lease shall automatically renew for successive twelve-month terms unless either party provides written notice of non-renewal no fewer than sixty days prior to expiration.
3. Lessee shall not sublet the Premises or any portion thereof without the prior written consent of Lessor, which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld.
output:
"""Here are the three clauses in plain language, with what each means for you in practice.

---

**1. Indemnification ("indemnify and hold harmless")**

> *Plain version:* If someone makes a claim against the landlord because of how you use the property, you have to cover it. That includes paying the landlord's legal costs and any money they owe.

**What this means for you:**
- Say a guest slips in your apartment, or your overflowing bathtub damages the unit below, and someone sues the landlord. You would be responsible for the cost.
- "Any and all claims" is broad. As written, it doesn't clearly exclude problems the landlord caused, such as a broken stair they failed to repair. Many states limit how far landlords can push this onto tenants, but the wording itself leans in the landlord's favor.
- **Tip:** This is a good reason to have **renter's insurance with liability coverage**. It's usually inexpensive. You could also ask the landlord to add *"except for claims caused by Lessor's negligence or misconduct."*

---

**2. Automatic renewal**

> *Plain version:* When your lease ends, it automatically renews for another full year, and keeps doing so every year. The only way to stop it is for you (or the landlord) to give **written** notice **at least 60 days before** the lease ends.

**What this means for you:**
- If you want to move out and you forget to give notice in time, you could be locked into **another full 12 months** of rent.
- A phone call or a casual text may not count. Send a letter or email you can prove was sent, and keep a copy.
- **Tip:** Right after signing, put a reminder in your calendar about **70–75 days before the lease end date** so you have time to decide and send notice.

---

**3. Subletting**

> *Plain version:* You can't rent out the place, or even part of it (like a spare room), to someone else unless the landlord agrees in writing first. The landlord can't refuse without a good reason.

**What this means for you:**
- Before bringing in a subtenant or roommate who pays you rent, get the landlord's **written** approval.
- The landlord can't say no just because they feel like it. They need a legitimate reason, such as the proposed person having poor credit or a bad rental history.
- Even if you sublet, you are usually **still responsible** to the landlord for rent and damage if the subtenant doesn't pay or causes problems.
- Short-term rentals like Airbnb would almost certainly count as subletting under this clause.

---

**Quick summary before you sign:**
1. You're financially responsible for problems arising from your use of the place, so get renter's insurance.
2. The lease renews for a full year unless you give written notice 60+ days before it ends, so set a reminder.
3. No subletting without the landlord's written OK, though they can't refuse unreasonably.

*This is a plain-language explanation, not legal advice. Tenant protections vary by state and city. If anything worries you, a local tenant's rights organization or legal aid office can often review a lease for free, sometimes the same day.*"""
